extracted.intended_audience: academics, researchers, and grant-panel participants interested in how disciplinary cultures shape proposal evaluation and concepts of excellence
extracted.subtask_description: Describes how different academic disciplines (English, history, anthropology, philosophy, etc.) conceptualize and operationalize 'excellence' and the evaluative criteria used on funding panels, with examples of favored skills and common pitfalls. Useful for understanding what panels from different fields value when awarding fellowships/grants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excellence as a constructed, intersubjective judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Excellence is often viewed as a construction resulting from the interaction of panelists rather than an objective property of a proposal (e.g., “I think … we have some kind of consensus around what we like … and then we call them excellence”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panel decisions rely on agreed-on but subjective criteria; panels 'label' proposals as high quality via collaboration, discussion, advocacy, and persuasion. Expect variability across panels and disciplines; consensus-building processes matter as much as intrinsic merits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrity and rigor of research
rubrics_metrics.description: Research should show 'integrity of the research' and be 'based in some kind of rigorous testing' in terms of how work is collected and methodologies used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panelists look for rigorous testing of ideas, sound methodology, careful data collection, and truthful handling of evidence. Anti-patterns include superficial methods or 'clocking time' (doing minimal work without depth).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of thought and articulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Having 'very clear ways of articulating what it all means'—clarity in framing, argumentation, and explanation of relevance is essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposals should clearly state what the work means, why it matters, and how it contributes. Readability and lucid expression can affect reception; overly obscure or impenetrable prose undermines perceived quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and contribution to knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Work must explain 'what contributions it’s going to make' and demonstrate originality—'building on the work of others in very significant ways, perhaps branching out, expanding other important work.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panels assess whether the project offers new insights, advances the field, or substantially extends existing scholarship. Applicants should situate contributions relative to the larger body of knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mastery of disciplinary methods/criteria (doing your homework)
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowing the theoretical and critical literature on the subject signals competence: 'If somebody doesn’t know the theoretical and critical literature on their subject, that tells you they haven’t been doing their homework.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposals should demonstrate familiarity with field-specific standards, methods, and prior work. Failing to show this invites skepticism about preparedness and scholarship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marshalling of evidence, strength of argument, and persuasiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognizable evaluative markers include 'marshalling of evidence, strength of argument, persuasiveness, an element of flair, originality of argument.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are common, cross-disciplinary markers used even when reviewers disagree ideologically (e.g., grading papers). Proposals should present coherent, well-supported arguments and persuasive evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical grounding / careful archival work
rubrics_metrics.description: History values 'careful archival work' and an empirical grounding; research oriented to getting results with sources that can be tested for validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In fields like history, panels favor projects with verifiable, concrete sources and archival methods. Interpretation should be tied to material evidence subject to verification; weak or unverifiable evidence is a liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verifiability / availability of concrete information
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals grounded in a 'concrete body of information that you can assess' are preferred in some disciplines (e.g., history) because interpretation refers to material subject to certain kinds of verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make clear what empirical base supports claims and how findings can be checked. Projects lacking a verifiable evidentiary base are harder to evaluate and may be disadvantaged relative to empirically grounded work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of theory and theoretical acumen
rubrics_metrics.description: Theory is an essential skill—useful for bridging disciplinary boundaries and enabling cross-disciplinary conversation—but can polarize; some disciplines prize being 'theory-driven' while others resist it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use theory to illuminate and connect work to broader debates, but avoid jargonizing, credentializing, or overly abstruse formulations. Panels value theoretical awareness balanced with methodological soundness and communicative clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of theorizing with readability
rubrics_metrics.description: Scholars must 'balance theorizing with readability'—work that is too 'fancy' or 'too complicated' risks being unreadable and therefore loses impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for accessibility without sacrificing intellectual sophistication. Overly dense prose can reduce the persuasive power of a proposal; readability is a criterion in its own right.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discipline-appropriate evaluation (match of criteria to disciplinary norms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Judging a proposal requires panelists to have a sense of criteria appropriate to the applicant’s discipline; mismatches (applying history criteria to an English proposal) can disadvantage applicants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Articulate why chosen methods and evaluative standards are appropriate for your discipline. When interdisciplinary, explicitly justify methodological choices to help panelists apply suitable criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willingness to revise hypotheses / responsiveness to data
rubrics_metrics.description: Scholars should be 'willing to challenge their premises' and 'consider data even after you’re well along in a study that completely challenges ... the hypothesis you’ve been making.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panels favor investigators who demonstrate intellectual flexibility and responsiveness to new evidence rather than rigid adherence to initial hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicability to nonspecialists / interdisciplinarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Theory and disciplinary skills that allow scholars 'to communicate with nonspecialists about topics that cut across areas of expertise' can enlarge an audience and positively affect evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When projects are interdisciplinary, clearly explain terms and stakes for non-specialist reviewers. Showing cross-disciplinary relevance can be an advantage if accessibility is maintained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of empty jargon / excessive credentializing
rubrics_metrics.description: Anti-patterns noted include 'empty jargon,' 'jargonizing and credentializing,' and writing that would be 'dismissed as a bunch of junk' by empirical scholars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid opaque, fashion-driven terminology that obscures substance. Clear, evidence-based argumentation is favored over stylistic displays of theory that lack empirical or logical grounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceived prestige and field size effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Some fields (e.g., history, art history, certain philosophy) carry an a priori prestige or larger applicant pools, which affects award distributions; being in a smaller or less consensual field (e.g., contemporary English) can be disadvantageous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize structural factors beyond proposal quality—field norms, applicant volume, and disciplinary prestige shape competition. When possible, make the case for the wider significance and rigor of work coming from less-favored subfields.
